content.text: {"project_summary":"Roman engineers achieved remarkably consistent aqueduct gradients over long distances using simple optical surveying tools and iterative correction, documented primarily through Frontinus's administrative treatise and surviving archaeological gradient surveys.","research_question":"How did Roman engineers design aqueducts to maintain a consistent water gradient over tens of kilometers using only visual surveying tools?","important_statistics":[{"statistic":"The Aqua Claudia had an average gradient of approximately 0.14% over its length.","source_ids":["22222222-aaaa-4aaa-8aaa-222222222222"]}],"chronology":[],"open_questions":["Exactly how much on-site iterative correction was needed versus upfront survey accuracy is not settled by the sources collected."],"research_gaps":["No source in this batch directly describes chorobates measurement error rates, despite the tool being central to the how-question."],"suggested_script_angles":["Frame the video around Frontinus as an eyewitness administrator rather than a modern historian's summary","Contrast the precision of the Aqua Claudia survey data against the popular myth that Romans achieved perfect gradients on the first attempt"],"prohibited_unsafe_assertions":["Do not claim an exact total aqueduct count for Rome as settled fact -- the collected sources disagree/are unverified on this point."],"cited_source_ids":["22222222-aaaa-4aaa-8aaa-222222222222"]}
